title: Cool Blue
description: A cool blue grade in cool color grade work shifts the image toward steel, cyan, or moonlight blues across shadows and often midtones. Warmth, if it survives, is reserved for a practical or a face that the story wants to save.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: Cold institutions, night, or alienation live in this family. A hospital, a CIA office, a pre-dawn street: the air has no honey.
Skin goes toward porcelain or grey-pink. One tungsten desk lamp, if you allow it, becomes the only hearth.
It is the wrong tool when you are faking night with underexposed sun. That is Day for Night, a capture trick, not only a blue LUT.

It is the wrong tool for sculpted moon as a key on a dark set: Moonlight Gel is a lighting decision. It is also the wrong tool if the complementary split of Teal and Orange is what you actually wanted (warm skin, teal air, not an overall steel wash).

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Bias white balance or the grade toward high Kelvin in the mids and shadows. Hold or isolate a warm practical if the scene needs one hearth.
Keep skin just readable; full cyan faces look sick unless that is the line. Night windows and fluorescent rooms already help.
Prompt: Cool blue grade on [Subject], steel shadows, hospital or moonlight, warmth reserved for one practical if any.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it for cold institutions, night, or alienation: a lawyer in a glass tower at 5 a.m., a clinic corridor. Do not use it as a synonym for day-for-night, and do not steel every romance interior.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: The Bourne Ultimatum runs steel-green-blue through offices, streets, and stations so the institution never thaws. Michael Clayton uses cold corporate and night hues against the few warmer domestic scraps.
Grammar of withheld warmth, not a copied still.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is Teal and Orange (skin stays warm) or Day for Night (hard shadows from a high sun). The tell is peach faces against cyan, or daytime sky structure.
Fix: overall cool bias, maybe one warm practical, no high-sun day cues.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is cool blue in film?
It is an overall cool color grade: steel, cyan, or moonlight blues in shadows and mids. Warmth is scarce and usually limited to a chosen practical.
Cool Blue vs Teal and Orange
Teal-orange protects warm skin and splits the rest toward cyan. Cool blue chills the whole world, faces included unless you reserve one lamp. One is a complementary split. The other is a cold wash.
When should I use cool blue?
Use it for institutions, night, or alienation. Skip it when you needed complementary punch, sculpted moon lighting, or a day-for-night capture.
How do I prompt cool blue for AI image or video?
Write: Cool blue grade on [Subject], steel shadows, hospital or moonlight, warmth reserved for one practical if any. Forbid peach-and-teal complementary splits and obvious daytime sun.
